Name: tta_scaling_medimg
Title: Test-Time Augmentation Scaling Laws for Medical Image Classification: When More Views Beat Bigger Models
Short Hypothesis: For medical image classification, compact models (small CNNs, MLPs) equipped with systematic test-time augmentation (TTA) can match or exceed the accuracy of large pre-trained models using single-pass inference. The accuracy gain from TTA follows a power-law relationship with the number of augmentation views, and there exists a crossover point where small model + TTA matches large model performance at lower total compute cost. This challenges the default assumption that scaling model parameters is the only path to better performance.
Related Work: Test-time augmentation (TTA) is a well-known technique where multiple augmented versions of a test input are processed and their predictions aggregated. While TTA has been used since AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), systematic analysis of its scaling behavior remains sparse. Recent work on test-time compute scaling (Snell et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2024) demonstrates that allocating more compute at inference can dramatically improve reasoning in LLMs, but this principle has not been systematically studied for vision classifiers. MedMNIST (Yang et al., 2023) provides standardized medical imaging benchmarks enabling controlled comparison. Foundation models like ViT and DINOv2 show strong transfer but their inference cost is rarely compared against simpler models with TTA. Recent findings that TabPFN does not consistently outperform simple ML baselines on clinical tasks (MedRxiv 2026) and that deep learning gene perturbation models fail to beat linear baselines (Nature Methods 2025) suggest the 'bigger is better' assumption deserves scrutiny in medical AI.
Abstract: We investigate test-time augmentation (TTA) scaling laws for medical image classification across MedMNIST benchmarks. While large pre-trained models dominate leaderboards, we hypothesize that compact models with systematic TTA can match their accuracy at lower total compute. We train models of varying capacity -- from logistic regression to ResNet-18 -- on PathMNIST, DermaMNIST, and BloodMNIST, then apply TTA with 1 to 100 augmented views. We measure accuracy as a function of view count and compare geometric, intensity, and mixed augmentation strategies with mean, majority vote, and confidence-weighted aggregation. Our experiments reveal power-law relationships between TTA view count and accuracy gain, identify crossover points where compact models with TTA match large model single-pass accuracy, and analyze calibration effects via Expected Calibration Error. The findings challenge the assumption that bigger models are always better and have practical implications for resource-constrained medical AI deployment, where inference cost per patient matters as much as raw accuracy.
Experiments: 1. Baseline Establishment: Train Logistic Regression (on flattened pixels), 2-layer MLP (hidden=256), Small CNN (3 conv layers), and ResNet-18 on PathMNIST (pathology, 9 classes), DermaMNIST (dermatology, 7 classes), and BloodMNIST (blood cell, 8 classes) from MedMNIST v2 (via the medmnist Python package). Use standard train/val/test splits. Report single-pass test accuracy, AUC, and model parameter count for each.

2. TTA Scaling Curves: For each trained model, apply TTA with N augmented views in {1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100}. Use mixed augmentations (random horizontal/vertical flip, rotation up to 15 degrees, color jitter brightness=0.2 contrast=0.2, random resized crop with scale 0.8-1.0). Aggregate via mean softmax probabilities. Plot accuracy vs N for each model-dataset combination. Fit power-law curves to the scaling behavior.

3. Augmentation Strategy Comparison: At N=50 views, compare three augmentation families: (a) geometric only (flip, rotate, crop), (b) intensity only (brightness, contrast, Gaussian noise sigma=0.05), (c) mixed (all combined). Also compare aggregation methods: mean softmax, majority vote, confidence-weighted (weight by max softmax). Report accuracy for all strategy-aggregation combinations.

4. Crossover Analysis: For each dataset, find the minimum N where SmallCNN+TTA(N) accuracy >= ResNet-18 single-pass accuracy. Estimate FLOPs for each configuration (model forward pass * N views) and plot compute-accuracy Pareto frontiers. Identify the compute-optimal strategy.

5. Calibration Analysis: Compute Expected Calibration Error (ECE, 15 bins) before and after TTA at N={1, 10, 50, 100} for all models. Plot ECE vs N to assess whether TTA improves not just accuracy but also uncertainty calibration -- critical for clinical deployment.
Risk Factors and Limitations: TTA may yield diminishing returns for models that are already well-calibrated or for easy classification tasks, limiting the generality of power-law scaling.
MedMNIST images are 28x28 pixels, which constrains the augmentation space compared to full-resolution clinical images. Results may not transfer to higher-resolution medical imaging.
The compute comparison uses FLOPs estimation which may not perfectly reflect wall-clock inference time differences due to batching and GPU parallelism effects.
Power-law scaling may only hold over a limited range of N values before saturation, and the crossover point may not exist for all model-dataset combinations.
Results are specific to classification tasks and may not generalize to detection, segmentation, or other medical imaging tasks.
The augmentation strategies tested are general-purpose; domain-specific medical augmentations (e.g., stain normalization for pathology) might yield different scaling behavior.
